nameStory: The splitgill mushroom gets its name from its unique gills that split down the middle when dry conditions arrive. Unlike regular mushroom gills that stay solid, these clever 'split-gills' can actually open and close like tiny accordions depending on humidity levels!
description: This small but fascinating fungus looks like a miniature Chinese fan made of tightly packed coral waves. The splitgill mushroom creates fan-shaped or bracket-like caps that are typically 1-4 centimeters wide with a creamy yellow to pale white color. Its most distinctive feature is its unusual gills that can actually split apart lengthwise, giving this common wood-decomposer its memorable name. Despite its small size, it's incredibly hardy and can be found year-round on dead wood.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: The signature split gills that open and close like tiny fans - they appear folded when moist but split apart to show their forked structure when dry

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small fan or bracket-shaped caps, 1-4 cm wide, with a fuzzy, dense yet spongy texture that feels almost felt-like to touch

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Creamy yellow to pale white color with wavy, undulating edges that resemble ocean waves frozen in time

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Usually stemless or with a very short, lateral attachment point where it connects to wood

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Generally odorless or with a faint, pleasant mushroomy smell - nothing unpleasant or distinctive

habitat: Look for splitgill mushrooms on dead hardwood branches, logs, and stumps throughout New England's forests, parks, and even urban areas. They're particularly common on oak, maple, and birch wood, thriving in both shaded woodlands and sunny edge habitats. You'll often find clusters of these small fans growing in overlapping groups on the same piece of rotting wood.

seasonality.spring: Fresh caps begin emerging on dead wood as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. Look for bright, creamy-colored specimens with tightly closed gills.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with abundant fresh fruiting bodies appearing after rain showers. The gills actively open and close based on daily humidity changes.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting on newly fallen branches and logs. Older specimens may appear more weathered and grayish but are still identifiable by their split gill structure.
seasonality.winter: Remarkably persistent through winter months, though growth slows significantly. Old caps become tough and leathery but retain their characteristic fan shape and split gills.

funFact: The splitgill mushroom is one of the most widespread fungi on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica, and can actually survive being completely dried out for months before springing back to life with the next rainfall!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small bracket fungi or turkey tail mushrooms, but the split gills are the dead giveaway - no other mushroom has gills that literally split down the middle. Memory trick: 'Split name, split gills!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'gill mushroom,' the splitgill's unique gill structure is so unusual that it's been placed in its own special family, separate from typical gilled mushrooms. This highlights how appearances can be deceiving in the fungal world.
compareHints: The splitgill is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique among our local fungi. When comparing to similar small bracket fungi like turkey tail or false turkey tail, focus on the gill structure underneath - splitgill is the only one with actual gills rather than pores or a smooth surface. The moveable, split gills are completely distinctive in our region.
